Construction began in 1929, and the Adler Planetarium opened to the public in May 1930. Its central instrument, a Zeiss projector, cast images of stars onto the inside of a dome. The projector did not display photographs of the night sky. Instead, its precisely arranged lenses reproduced the positions and brightness of thousands of stars. This technology allowed audiences to experience a convincing simulation of the heavens even during daylight.

Over subsequent decades, Adler staff expanded the institution beyond its original theater. They added exhibits, telescopes, and educational programs for students and families. The building underwent a major renovation in 1999, which created new exhibition spaces and improved the theater. Today, the Adler continues to combine traditional sky shows with interactive displays about astronomy and space exploration.

Later, seeds carried by ocean currents or birds established grasses and shrubs. By 1908, researchers had recorded more than two dozen plant species on the island. Rather than simply listing the species, the researchers noted where each one grew and when it first appeared. These records allowed scientists to trace a gradual sequence from simple pioneer communities to denser vegetation.

In the following decades, trees began to shade out many of the grasses that had arrived earlier. Animals also returned, feeding on the plants and carrying additional seeds between distant parts of the island. By comparing surveys made at different times, ecologists could see that an ecosystem develops through both replacement and interaction. Krakatau therefore became one of the best-known natural laboratories for the study of ecological succession.
